\[
r_s = \frac{\tan(r\, \theta_m)}{\tan \theta_m},
\qquad \theta_m = \frac{ 120^{\circ} }{2}
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(r\): The distance of an output pixel from the image center, as a share of half the diagonal
- \(r_s\): The distance of the source position it reads, in the same unit
- \(\theta_m\): Half the field of view

An equidistant fisheye lens maps the angle theta of a ray to an image radius proportional to theta, one of the projections that Kannala and Brandt describe. A normal, rectilinear lens maps it to a radius proportional to tan theta. The filter treats the image as a rectilinear view with the same diagonal field and redraws it as an equidistant fisheye. A pixel at radius r shows the ray at angle r theta_m, which the source shows at tan(r theta_m) / tan(theta_m). Near the center r_s is less than r, so the center is enlarged, while the corners stay where they are. Each output pixel reads the source at the mapped position with bilinear interpolation, the inverse mapping of Gonzalez and Woods, so no holes appear.
